mainTopic: Protecting documents from forgery: cut-off signatures in a מקושר, and רבי יוחנן's rules on erasures and the last line of a שטר
overview: Earlier on the page, the גמרא worried about a forger who cuts off the last line of a מקושר (a tied document), taking the first part of a witness's signature with it. If the witness signed 'ראובן בן יעקב עד', what is left reads 'יעקב עד' and looks like a full signature. The amud opens with the end of the answer: the court can tell this is not the real signature of anyone named יעקב. The גמרא then asks whether the witness might have signed with his father's name, or used it as a personal mark, the way some חכמים signed with drawings or single letters. Both ideas are rejected, because people do not treat their father's name that way. מר זוטרא then gives a simpler solution: in a מקושר all the signatures must end on the same line, so cutting a line would damage every signature and expose the forgery. Next, רבי יוחנן gives two rules for scribes. Every erasure in a שטר must be confirmed at the end with 'וְדֵין קִיּוּמֵיהוֹן', and the last line must repeat some of the document's content. The amud ends with the גמרא asking the reason for this second rule, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The court knows it is not יעקב's signature
steps.stepSummary: This line finishes the earlier answer. The remaining 'יעקב' is recognized as not being the real signature of anyone named יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to the forgery worry. The court will see that the leftover name 'יעקב' does not match the real signature of any witness named יעקב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forger hoped that 'יעקב עד' would pass as a complete signature. But a signature can be checked: if no known יעקב signs this way, the court realizes a line was cut off. The forgery fails because signatures are recognizable.

keyTerms.meaning: the father's name left over after the cut, here mistaken for the witness's own name
a 'tied' document, folded and stitched, with the witnesses signing on the back between the folds

phrases.english: It is not Yaakov's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to the forgery concern raised just before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual recognition: the court can check whether the signature belongs to a real person named יעקב.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A cut-off signature reading 'יעקב עד' might pass as a valid witness signature.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court knows no יעקב signs this way, so it realizes the document was cut.

steps.title: Maybe the witness signed with his father's name
steps.stepSummary: Challenge: perhaps the witness really did sign only 'יעקב', using his father's name instead of his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe he signed using his father's name!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer. Maybe 'יעקב' is a real, complete signature, because the witness chose to sign with his father's name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a witness might sign with his father's name, then 'יעקב עד' could be genuine. The court could no longer say 'this is not יעקב's signature', because it might be the son's way of signing. That would make it impossible to spot the forgery.

phrases.english: But perhaps he signed with his father's name!
phrases.notes: 'He' is the witness whose signature was cut. Maybe 'יעקב' really is his whole signature.

steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the court can tell the signature is not יעקב's.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a son might sign with his father's name, the leftover 'יעקב' could be a genuine signature, and the forgery could not be detected.

steps.title: People do not drop their own name for their father's
steps.stepSummary: Answer: no one leaves out his own name and signs only with his father's name.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person does not leave out his own name and sign with his father's name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the challenge. People simply do not sign that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer is based on normal human behavior. Since no one signs only with his father's name, a signature reading 'יעקב' alone must be cut off. Step 1's answer stands.

phrases.english: A person does not leave out his own name,
and sign with his father's name.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to how people normally behave.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A witness might sign with his father's name alone.
steps.terutzMaskana: People always include their own name, so a signature of just 'יעקב' shows a cut.

steps.title: Maybe the name is just his personal mark
steps.stepSummary: New challenge: maybe the witness uses the name 'יעקב' as his own signature mark, the way famous חכמים signed with pictures or single letters.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe it is just a sign he made for himself! After all, רב drew a fish, רבי חנינא drew a palm branch, רב חסדא wrote a סמך, רב הושעיא wrote an עין, and רבא בר רב הונא drew a ship's mast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries again. Maybe the witness is not 'signing with his father's name' at all. Maybe 'יעקב' is simply the mark he always uses, and it gives examples of חכמים who signed with marks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a sharper version of step 2. It does not claim he signs with his father's name; it claims he uses it as a symbol, like a drawing. Since real people did sign with symbols, the leftover 'יעקב' might be a genuine signature mark.

phrases.english: But perhaps it is just a sign that he made it!
phrases.notes: He means the witness made the name 'יעקב' into his personal signature mark.

phrases.english: For Rav would draw a fish,
Rabbi Chanina would draw a palm branch,
Rav Chisda, a samekh,
phrases.notes: He signed with just the letter ס.

phrases.english: Rav Hoshaya, an ayin,
Rava bar Rav Huna, a ship's mast!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 3 rejected 'signing with his father's name', this offers a different way the name 'יעקב' could be a genuine signature.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a lone 'יעקב' must mean the signature was cut.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Real חכמים signed with symbols, so a witness could use a name as his symbol, and then 'יעקב' might be genuine.

steps.title: No one would be so disrespectful to his father
steps.stepSummary: Answer: a person would not be so bold as to turn his father's name into a signature mark.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person is not so bold as to make his father's name into a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the second challenge. Using your father's name as a mere mark would be disrespectful, and people do not do it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Drawings and letters are fine as marks, but a father's name is different. Treating it as a doodle-style symbol is insolent. So the leftover 'יעקב' still shows the document was cut.

phrases.english: A person is not so bold as to make
his father's name into a sign.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא חֲצִיף אִינָשׁ לְשַׁוּוֹיֵהּ לִשְׁמֵיהּ דַּאֲבוּהּ סִימָנָא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to respect for parents and normal behavior.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A witness might use his father's name as a personal mark, like the חכמים' drawings.
steps.terutzMaskana: No one treats his father's name that disrespectfully, so step 1's answer stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The first approach blocks the forgery by recognizing signatures. A lone 'יעקב' cannot be real, because people neither sign with their father's name nor use it as a mark.

steps.title: מר זוטרא: all signatures must end on one line
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא gives a simpler fix. A מקושר whose witnesses' signatures do not all end on the same line is invalid, so cutting a line would damage every signature and expose the forgery.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said: Why do you need all this? Any מקושר whose witnesses do not end on one line is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא says the whole back-and-forth is unnecessary. He gives a rule that solves the forgery problem directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion assumed the witnesses sign one under the other, so cutting the bottom line would damage only one signature. מר זוטרא says the signatures must all line up and end at the same line. Cutting that line would cut every signature, so the forgery would be obvious, and a document that is not lined up this way is invalid anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: why do you need all this?

steps.confusionAlert: מר זוטרא is not saying the earlier answers were wrong. He is saying they are not needed, because the signing rule itself prevents this forgery.
steps.whyThisMatters: It turns a problem about detecting forgeries into a rule about how a מקושר must be signed. A badly signed tied document is invalid from the start.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra said:
Why do you need all this?
Any tied document whose witnesses
do not end on one line is invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא אָמַר לְמָה לָךְ כּוּלֵּי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets aside the whole defense in steps 1-5 and offers a simpler, rule-based solution to the same forgery concern.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A structural rule about how signatures must be arranged, which makes the forgery impossible to hide.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Witnesses sign one under another, so a forger could cut one signature and we would need to recognize handwriting to catch him.
steps.terutzMaskana: All signatures must end on the same line. Otherwise the document is invalid, and any cut would damage all the names visibly.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מקושר whose witnesses' signatures do not end on a single line is invalid.

steps.title: Two rules for a scribe writing a document
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that every erasure in a שטר must be confirmed at the end with 'וְדֵין קִיּוּמֵיהוֹן', and that the scribe must repeat some of the document's content in the last line.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יצחק בר יוסף said in the name of רבי יוחנן: For all erasures in a document, the scribe must write 'And this is their verification.' He must also repeat some of the content of the document in the last line.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רבי יוחנן with two practical rules for how a scribe writes a שטר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rule one covers erasures. If something in the שטר was erased and corrected, the scribe must confirm it at the end of the document so nobody can claim it was changed later. Rule two says the last line must repeat some of what the document already said, instead of bringing new information.

keyTerms.meaning: Erasures: places in the document where writing was scraped off and corrected
'And this is their verification': the closing line that confirms the erasures
A legal document, such as a loan or sale document
The last line of the document, right before the witnesses sign
That he should go back and repeat

steps.confusionAlert: These are two separate rules. The first is about erasures. The second, repeating content in the last line, applies to every document, even one with no erasures at all.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
For all erasures, every one of them,
he must write 'And this is their verification.'
phrases.notes: At the end of the document, the scribe confirms each erased spot and what the corrected words say.

phrases.english: And he must repeat some of the content of the document
in the last line;

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching about how documents are written. It continues the general theme of protecting a שטר from forgery.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every erasure must be confirmed at the end with 'וְדֵין קִיּוּמֵיהוֹן', and the last line of a שטר must repeat earlier content from the document.

steps.title: Asking the reason for repeating content in the last line
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the scribe must repeat the document's content in the last line.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the rule it just heard. This line is setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a real question asking for information, not an attack on רבי יוחנן. It sits right after the second rule, so it is asking why the last line must repeat what the document already said.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason? The standard way of asking for the logic behind a rule

phrases.english: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: This asks about the second rule, repeating content in the last line.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the second rule of רבי יוחנן in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why must the scribe repeat some of the document's content in the last line?
